subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house may desire that I should make a short report on the constitutional conference which ended yesterday afternoon, and which I think successfully began the process of reshaping our constitution by federal-provincial co-operation, which is of course the only way it can be done.
At the beginning, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I may be permitted to pay a tribute to the officials of the federal government who did so much of the preparatory work, and did it so well. As the house may know, some weeks ago a special secretariat was set up to work on this problem. That secretariat consisted of officials of the government, whom I will not mention by name, who did their work with that distinction, efficiency and devotion which we expect to receive and do receive from the Canadian civil service.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
They were greatly assisted by three distinguished experts in the field of constitutional law who gave their time to the work of the secretariat. Perhaps I could mention them by name, Dr. Carl Goldenberg and Professors Head and Strayer. We are very grateful to them for the work they did, which was of great value to the federal participation in the conference and which will be of great value in the work ahead.
The conference decided, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps this is the most important agreement that was reached, to undertake a comprehensive review of the constitution of Canada with the objective of introducing whatever changes may be agreed to be necessary to make it adequate to meet the problems of Canada today and in the future. The conference also agreed that the heads of the governments of Canada, who are responsible to the
people of Canada, should and would assume responsibility for this review. To this end there will be further sessions of the constitutional conference as required.
To ensure that the work is carried forward without delay and is effectively co-ordinated in accordance with the directions of the conference, the conference agreed on the establishment of a continuing constitutional committee consisting of senior advisers qualified in this field and designated by each government, the federal government and the provincial governments.
The constitutional conference and the committee will be assisted by a secretariat to be provided by the federal government, but to which members will be nominated by the provincial governments if they so desire. We will be getting in touch with the provincial governments at once with a view to receiving nominations from those governments to this central secretariat. The continuing committee of officials is authorized to set up sub-committees on specific questions, with the approval of the constitutional conference.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
It was also agreed that the following questions should be examined by committees set up for that purpose under the authorization of the constitutional conference and the continuing committee of officials. First, the question of official languages; I will return to that in a moment. Second, the question of fundamental human rights. The federal government submitted a charter of human rights on this subject which received support from four provincial governments for enshrinement in a constitution of Canada, and it was agreed that a special committee should go into this whole subject. Third, a committee on the distribution of powers. This is a fundamental aspect of the whole question. Fourth, reform of institutions linked with federalism, including the Senate and the Supreme Court of Canada. Fifth, the problem of regional disparities which received consideration at the conference. Sixth, the question of amending procedure and provisional arrangements. Finally-and this is broader than the question of constitutional change-the whole question

February 8, 1988
Canadian Constitution
of federal-provincial machinery for consultation.
As I am sure hon. members know, the conference discussed at some length the recommendations of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism with regard to linguistic and cultural equality. I think those of us who took part in the meeting of this conference can be grateful that this report was before us. It seems to me that it alone is abundant justification for the work done by this royal commission. On this subject the conference agreed on the following paragraphs as recommendations of the conference which will be before the special committee dealing with the subject.
First, recognition by this conference that, as proposed by the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism and as a matter of equity, French speaking Canadians outside of Quebec should have the same rights as English speaking Canadians in Quebec.
Second, recognition, as the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism has recommended, of the desirability of proceeding by government action as speedily as possible in ways most appropriate in each province and without diminishing existing rights recognized by law or usage.
Third, establishment of a special committee to examine the report of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism and the views expressed at this conference on this report and on other matters relating to language rights and their effective provision in practice, and to consult on methods of implementation, including the nature of possible federal assistance, and on the form and the method of constitutional amendment.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the main subjects that were discussed at the conference. I do not intend to give any exhaustive review of this conference this afternoon or to outline what it accomplished in the constitutional and political development of this country. I think it was a very good first step in federal-provincial consideration of this vital subject. The position of the federal government in relation to the matter generally was set out in a booklet "Federalism for the Future" which was circulated to members of the conference and which, if the house agrees, I would be glad to table in English and French at this time.
If it is agreeable to the house I am sure it would be useful to arrange for a day's debate, perhaps next week, on this whole question of constitutional change and the federalism of the future. If this could be done by general

agreement the whole matter could then be discussed at greater length.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the Conservative party and Her Majesty's loyal opposition share the feeling of satisfaction which we believe is felt all across the country that this conference, concluded yesterday, has had a significant measure of success and that its results represent an encouraging step forward on the way to perfecting a grand design for the second century of Canadian confederation.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
For his part in convening the conference and for his conduct of it as chairman, credit is due to the Prime Minister of Canada. We wished him well on its eve; its success was important for the welfare of Canada, and we are happy to record our appreciation of his part now that it is over. There is no doubt that his conciliatory attitude and experience were of real value in helping the conference to surmount one or two difficult and awkward moments.
Remarkable and encouraging, especially coming as it did practically in the opening moments, was the degree of unanimity expressed on the matter of language rights. While there were some important differences, credit is surely due to those who, being most fundamentally concerned, such as the prime minister of Ontario, accepted so clearly and so calmly the responsibility for the pattern of the future in this area.

It should be emphasized, I think, that in the field of linguistic rights, the provinces are primarily responsible, as pointed out by the Quebec premier, Mr. Johnson, among others. There are, therefore, numerous points to be discussed and settled before an agreement can be reached, and any progress will depend, to a great extent, on the points on which the provinces will agree. We trust that the federal government will be willing to carry out its commitments, that is, to help the provinces in that field, if required.

It is noted, Mr. Speaker, that the conference made no mention of the position of those
February 8, 1968

Canadians whose mother tongue is neither French nor English. This is a matter which the provinces, therefore, may well have to consider in the committee, perhaps on the basis set out in the government white paper which we believe probably expresses the views they actually hold.
While we can take satisfaction, in this area and others, for what progress there was, it would not be realistic if we overlooked the fact that in order to find solutions we have still very much further to go than the distance we have come. In two of the most important areas especially, the examination of the division of constitutional powers and a program to deal with regional economic differences, little more was accomplished than a preliminary statement of position. Important though that be, it certainly means that most of the practical work lies ahead. Clearly, too, with respect to the division of powers, the width of the gap between two of the positions was also demonstrated.
I express the hope that there will be no intransigence in the working out of details, so the committee set up to work in this area may be allowed to approach its task in the spirit of good will and dedication that is so vital to success. It is obvious that a great deal remains to be done in the way of mutual exchanges of opinions, education as to each other's points of view, and efforts to bring them into reconciliation. It is important that we assist the country to understand its various parts.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
In this matter of understanding, just as in the field of practical and acceptable redivisions or transfers of power, may I emphasize that there can be, in our view, no one way streets. This must be a two way traffic.
Here I must make a serious suggestion to the Prime Minister and to the house. Before I come to that, however, we desire to record our regret that it was not seen fit or possible to include representatives of the Yukon as delegates at this conference. We also record our very real desire to see progress made in the immediate future in constitutional advancement in that territory.
The whole of Canada's constitutional arrangements are, of course, of concern to the parliament of Canada, but no two areas are of more concern than the two I have mentioned, the division of powers and the closing of the gaps of economic differences between our regions. That is what confederation is all about. These are fields of interest essentially
Canadian Constitution
involving federal interest and concern. There can be no question, therefore, that they are matters of primary concern for the parliament of Canada.
I must therefore express our concern that there should be set up without further delay adequate arrangements for meaningful discussion of these matters by parliament, and for effective consultation between the government and parliament before final positions in these various fields are taken by the government.
I note that the Prime Minister has indicated the possibility of setting aside a day next week to discuss these matters. I feel this will be welcome, but express a reservation in this respect. It will be appreciated that this is the first time the Prime Minister has mentioned the matter. My reservation is that in the light of the seriousness of this whole matter and its enormous scope, one day's debate may not be adequate. I say this because we take the firm position that after all this is the parliament of all Canada; this is the forum in which the views of those who speak for all Canada can be collectively expressed; and this is the body, therefore, which should and indeed must be fully consulted before commitments are made in this field.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It will not be enough to say after agreement is made in committee or at the conference, "Oh, we will refer it to you for approval at that time", because such agreement can only be arrived at on the basis of a commitment by the government of Canada. Such a commitment should, in our view, only be made after consultation here.
Accordingly, while I note that the Prime Minister has referred to a day's debate and has also implied that a parliamentary committee may be appointed, we ask for a definite commitment and urge that such a committee be appointed just as early as possible. The government will find this party, which has repeatedly urged this course, ready to serve and work with our colleagues in other parts of parliament on such a committee just as soon as it can appropriately be constituted.
In connection with the process of education, consultation and reconciliation which is so essential to success in the constitutionmaking process, I should like to repeat the view we have expressed before, that the greater the extent to which such meetings are held in public, the greater the advantage to Canada. I am certain there will be agreement

February 8, 1968
Canadian Constitution
that this was amply demonstrated as a result of the extent of public awareness and interest in the proceedings of the conference just concluded. I should like to congratulate all the governments on their initiative in this respect. I hope the same policy will be followed with respect to meetings of our parliamentary committee and with respect to further meetings of the governments in constitutional conferences.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like on behalf of this party to express our appreciation to the members of the other governments concerned who took part in this conference and submitted their views and positions to the scrutiny of public examination. I would like to pay special tribute to the prime minister of Ontario, not only for his participation in and manner at the conference just concluded, but also for his farsighted Canadianism in the preliminary conference or confederation of tomorrow which he called and which was held in Toronto last November. It is not my purpose to be critical-the conference here has been a success-but many millions of Canadians share the view that the gapfilling initiative of Prime Minister Robarts was a prerequisite to that success.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative party shares in the general satisfaction about the marked success of this conference, especially the contribution made by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) and by all those who took part in it. We trust that the measures taken immediately to ensure consultations with parliament will not only acknowledge the concern and responsibility of that institution, but will also contribute, to a large extent, to the successful strengthening of confederation, so dear to us all.

subtopic: REPORT BY PRIME MINISTER ON FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those of us who were invited and were privileged to attend the constitutional conference which ended yesterday had a feeling that we were taking part in an event which was of tremendous historical consequence for our country and its future.
I want to join the hon. member for Kamloops in expressing my personal appreciation, not only as a member of parliament but simply as a Canadian, for the way in which the Prime Minister presided over that conference with wit and wisdom and the flexibility

which were necessary if the conference was to succeed at all. I am sure I can say without any exaggeration that the success it did achieve was due to the manner and way in which he chaired the discussions, particularly when they became a little thorny at certain times.
In view of the fact that we are to have a debate on the subject I need not speak for too long, but permit me to make the following points. Some of them will imply some criticism, but I intend to make them merely to underline my belief that if we are to hold our country together and develop a viable constitution relevant to our day, then rigidity must go and flexibility must take its place. When the confederation of tomorrow conference was first called, the reaction of some leaders of the party on the other side of the house was very lukewarm and almost unfriendly. It became absolutely clear during the last three days that the initiative taken by the premiers of the provinces of Canada was not only necessary but an indispensable prelude to the discussions which took place this week.
The second point I want to make, from which it seems to me we ought to learn, is that for a very long time the attitude of certain important spokesmen in this parliament was against the concept that it was necessary to have a comprehensive review of the constitution. What in effect they said to the people of Canada and to the members of parliament was that all we need to do is concern ourselves with the language rights and perhaps with other human rights, but that when these matters have been dealt with the problem facing Canada at present will solve itself and there will be no need for a total or comprehensive review of the constitution.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
It became perfectly clear from the first hour of the conference that there was a need to be concerned with a comprehensive review of the constitution. In his statement yesterday the Prime Minister said, on behalf of his government, that the federal government was in favour-I think this was the word, and I am taking it from memory so I will be corrected if I am wrong-of entering into a total review of the constitution. In the statement the right hon. gentleman made today he called it a comprehensive review.
It has been obvious to some of us for some time that this kind of review and study of what needs rearranging, what needs bringing up to date, was essential for the future of this
February 8, 1968

country. It was a great step forward when that was recognized and acknowledged, not by all the heads of government who were there because there were still one or two who questioned it, but by the vast majority of heads of government who were there. I think, Mr. Speaker, now that the federal government has taken the initiative one can rest assured that it will continue that initiative. I hope, as the hon. member for Kamloops said, we will be prepared to discuss all aspects of the constitution and all phases of our federal-provincial arrangements as well as the rights of Canadians everywhere.
I was particularly glad, Mr. Speaker, as were my colleagues the leader of my party and the hon. member for Greenwood, who attended the conference as observers for this party, to note that the majority of the heads of provincial governments were prepared to accept the principles set out in the first volume of the B and B report. Furthermore, and to me this was even more important as I am sure it was to others, not only did they accept the principles but in the case of Ontario, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan if I remember correctly, and Nova Scotia, steps had already been taken to put into practical effect the application of those principles. I feel that without regard to the party or the politics involved, the people of Canada ought to be grateful to the governments of those provinces, whatever their political stripe, for having been imaginative enough to take these steps even before the conference was held, and to give the undertakings that are essential for a united Canada in the future.
Our leader said, of course, when the B and B volume was tabled that we gave full support in principle to the recommendations in that volume, and we still do. We are in full support also of the idea of entrenching a charter of human rights in the constitution, even though that came up against some difficulties. We hope they are only temporary difficulties, and that eventually the constitutional conference will agree to making that a fact.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman reported, and of course correctly, that on his suggestion the conference which met on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of this week has been, as it were, declared a continuing constitutional conference consisting of the heads of governments. It is obvious you 27053-4095
Canadian Constitution
cannot make essential, fundamental constitutional revisions without the consent or acceptance of the people of Canada. It is obvious, too, that the heads of governments are the only ones who can take part in such discussions and make commitments. I am sure it is agreed that unless the people of Canada everywhere are prepared to accept these revisions at some point or other, we will have great difficulty.
I congratulate the Prime Minister, therefore, and the premiers of the provinces for two things, in my opinion both equally important. The first is that the conference was open so the people of Canada could participate in the discussions; and second, that observers from the opposition parties were invited to attend so that members of this parliament might have first hand experience of the proceedings. I hope this arrangement will continue at future meetings of this conference.
The final point I should like to make, Mr. Speaker, is one we have made many times. My leader and the hon. member for Greenwood have asked many times that a parliamentary committee be appointed without delay, and that it be given the opportunity to study fully all the implications and all the suggestions made from all quarters. I want to join the hon. member for Kamloops in pressing the Prime Minister not to delay the appointment of such a committee. Such a committee will have sense enough, I am sure, not to attempt to reach rapid conclusions or to lay down firm guide lines. We are all aware of the fact that constitutional revision is a matter for lengthy discussion and temperate debate, but the sooner members of this parliament begin to consider this problem in depth collectively, the better will be the chance that what the government is able to accomplish will have the support of this parliament as a whole.
I congratulate the Prime Minister on the success that has been achieved so far. As he indicated by a story he told, it is only a first step. We are all aware of the great difficulties still ahead. We all have confidence in the desire of all Canadians and all governments to see this country united and stronger, and any revisions of the constitution necessary to achieve that end will undoubtedly be agreed to in time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were informed today that a government in another country has resigned because

February 8. 1968
Canadian Constitution
of its inability to solve a language problem. I think we should thank the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) for having proposed this federal-provincial conference on the language problem which concerns us so much in Canada today. This conference was intended to prevent in Canada what happened in other countries.
We see that Canada is not the only country with a language problem. We are indebted to the Canadian government and to the right hon. Prime Minister for having taken steps to ensure that this federal-provincial conference contribute to a better understanding between the premiers of the ten provinces, so that what has just happened in Belgium may be prevented from happening in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to thank the Prime Minister for taking the necessary steps so that the proceedings of that conference could unfold before all the Canadian people. Thus all Canadians were able to hear what went on between the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada as well as between them and some of their advisers. We noticed that those discussions were very frank and, as a matter of fact, the Canadian people were able to see what was happening and know what their repreesntatives thought.
Things are a little different from what they were 40 or 50 years ago when politicians could say something in one city and then make an entirely different speech in another city without the electors or the_ public being any the wiser. Through television, we have been able to show the general public all that happened during this conference.
As an observer for my party at the conference, I noted how easy it was for the Prime Minister, with his old diplomatic skill, to chair the proceedings of this conference. I believe that everyone present noted his skill. As a matter of fact, some even praised his ability in timing coffee breaks.
I agree with the Prime Minister that we should be grateful to the secretariat for being so helpful to all who attended, and we should not forget the maintenance men who had to mop up the floor and do some repairs at the very beginning of the conference. In spite of this mishap, the proceedings were a great step toward national unity.
I also noticed the unanimous agreement of all participants to what the right hon. Prime Minister suggested, that French-speaking Canadians receive the same treatment outside Quebec as that granted to English-speaking Canadians in Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I would

point out to the house that the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), leader of the Ralliement Creditiste, has been calling for just that for at least ten years. On many occasions, here in the house, he has called for French-speaking Canadians to receive the same treatment in the other provinces as that given to English-speaking Canadians in the province of Quebec. This is now recognized by all the premiers of the country. It shows that everyone, in his own area, is ready for a linguistic breakthrough and this portends better days for the two founding peoples of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Prime Minister's suggestion that a more exhaustive debate should be held on that matter next week. One day might be enough to enable each party's spokesman to express his views, provided however, as suggested by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) that a special committee be appointed to study the matter thoroughly.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister of Canada and the provincial premiers should be thanked for taking part in that conference and for agreeing to the establishment of a committee made up of high officials, in addition to a conference of premiers, responsible mainly for revising the Canadian constitution. That was the main objective of the federal-provincial conference, because obviously it was not the premiers' role to come to a conclusion during those three days; there was not enough time.
The committee of officials, who will have to make suggestions and advise the conference of premiers will have a beneficial effect. But I noticed, during these three days of discussions, that the provinces seemed to attach much more importance to equalization payments. That proves that the provinces are especially concerned with economic and financial problems. I understood that what the provinces need, most of them at least, is money. Therefore, I think that the committee of officials and the conference of premiers will be able to deal with all these subjects and that in the near future, suggestions will be made with a view to amending the constitution and do justice to all classes and all governments in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, we have listened with a great deal
February 8, 1988

of interest to the statement just made by the Prime Minister on the discussions at the conference that has just concluded. In view of the recommendation that a debate be held on this subject next week my remarks are going to be very brief.
I should just like to say that any and all attempts to resolve our problems and eliminate the frictions that affect our country are commendable. In this most recent conference matters of real concern were discussed both frankly and forcefully. It is far too early to assess the results of this conference. To some, viewing the prospects through spectacles rose tinted by hope and optimism, it might appear that there is clear sailing ahead. To others, who prefer to face the issues realistically, the problems and objectives outlined require careful analysis and sound thinking before conclusions are reached and decisions made.
I believe the obstacles on the path the government of Canada has chosen to follow are very real, and this is particularly true with respect to proposed amendments to the constitution. As pointed out in various briefs, in particular those submitted by the premiers of British Columbia and Alberta, attempts over the past years to find an acceptable formula for domiciling the constitution of Canada in Canada have thus far proved unsuccessful, and if this essential first step is impossible of achievement the consideration of further steps is somewhat premature.
This institution of parliament should clearly understand that the suggestions made by the federal government propose a definite shift from our traditional concept of legislative supremacy to one of constitutional supremacy with the ultimate power in the Supreme Court. It remains to be seen, Mr. Speaker, whether the Canadian people want such a change to be made.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPOSITION OF COINS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp for second reading of Bill No. S-23, to amend the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act and the Criminal Code.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPOSITION OF COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened last evening to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Chretien) give us an outline of the purpose behind the bill. I should like to suggest to the government, as I did by way of a question before the Christmas recess, a certain course of action which should be followed in the minting of coins, with particular reference to metallic or silver dollars as we have referred to them in the past. Even though they may be made of nickel this year I still have a tendency to call
6504	COMMONS
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins them silver dollars because that is the designation they have been given since 1935 when they were first minted in this country.
There is a way to mint dollars with a silver content and still make a rather handsome profit so tar as the operations of the mint are concerned. Up until last year silver coinage contained 800 parts of silver. In a silver dollar this amounted to 0.6 ounces of silver which, at the almost standard price until about a year ago of $1.29 per ounce, meant that each coin contained about 77.4 cents of silver.
I should like to refer to silver dollars for numismatic or collection purposes. Silver dollars minted in the past for general circulation and for use as currency have actually been used by people such as numismatists, collectors and others who put them away for their children or for other purposes. Very few of them have actually been used by people in the conduct of their business. Very few silver dollars minted in Canada since 1935 have ever got into general circulation. While I am talking particularly about silver coinage for numismatic purposes, what I have to say applies equally to the silver dollars that went into general circulation because, as I say, almost all of them end up being taken out of circulation rather than being used as currency.
The number of silver dollars minted in the past few years for numismatic pusposes, sold in sets or singly in a plastic cover, in 1964 amounted to approximately 2.85 million, in 1965 approximately 2.7 million, and in 1966 approximately 700,000 or slightly less. If we took a high average of about 2,500,000 silver dollars during a year and minted that many this year with a content of silver of 50 per cent, or 500 parts instead of 800 parts, we would have a substantial saving. This would be the same silver content as used in dimes and quarters during the latter part of last year. In terms of the maximum price for silver of about $2.30, which was about the peak last year, using 50 per cent silver in silver dollars we could mint them with a content value of 88.125 cents of silver.
I do not intend to go into these statistics in any greater detail except to point out to the government that in years past silver dollars of the numismatic type were sold for $1.25. They contained 77.4 cents of silver. In other words, the income in relation to the value of the silver showed a profit picture of 47.6 cents. If we made a silver dollar this year

DEBATES	February 8, 1988
with a 50 per cent silver content and distributed it to numismatists, collectors, dealers and others for $2 instead of $1.25 we would bring in at least $1 to the coffers of the government for each silver dollar sold.
The minister says it is not possible to do this because it is difficult to obtain silver as it is being used for other purposes including the space program in the United States, the film industry and the like. Late last year I checked to see if it was possible to obtain silver in quantity. I found it would have been possible on a long term purchase contract to obtain sufficient amounts of silver for use in silver dollars. It may not be too late even now to purchase the silver. As I listened to the Minister of National Revenue I understood him to say there was a provision in a schedule to this bill whereby dollars may be minted with a silver content as well as of pure nickel. The minister would be well advised to make inquiries into this suggestion of minting silver dollars this year with a 50 per cent silver content to be sold for $2 each. Not one single silver dollar, I submit, would end up in general circulation. They would end up in the possession of collectors or people who put them away to commemorate a certain anniversary. The mint and the federal treasury would end up with a substantial profit by minting silver dollars this year in this way.
It may be that at some time in the future it will be impossible to mint silver coins but it certainly would be possible to do so this year. This year is the sixtieth anniversary of the mint. I understand the mint is preparing a presentation case which will contain the nickel dollar and that it is a beautifully designed article. Even though nickel is a shiny substance and withstands wear for a long period of time, as suggested by the Minister of National Revenue last night, it cannot possibly equal the brilliance and lustre of silver. It would seem to me that the two together, a silver dollar and the presentation case that is being prepared by the mint in any event, would make an ideal collectors' item this year to commemorate the diamond jubilee, the sixtieth anniversary of the mint. There are a few other items to which I wish to refer but I think it might be more appropiate to deal with them when we get to the committee stage.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPOSITION OF COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that this bill comes at the right time
February 8, 19G8	COMMONS DEBATES	6505
since, in my opinion, it is indirectly connected with national unity and it can therefore be considered as complementary to the federal-provincial conference which has just ended.
Currency, which appears often in this bill, is a subject of interest to all Canadians from sea to sea. All classes of society are interested in currency. All governments, federal, provincial or municipal, are interested in currency. Political parties also are interested in currency, whether they be a left-wing, right-wing or centre party. In fact, we are all interested in it.
The passing of this bill will make it possible not only to change the size of some coins but to use nickel instead of silver. Currency, up to now, consisted of a silver alloy. If silver is a precious metal, nickel is not less shiny.
In view of the fact that our country ranks first in the world among nickel producers, obviously the government can consider making a few changes without fearing that it will lack metal.
However, what is of special interest to me is the price at which the coins will be sold: at what price will the twenty-five cent, flfty-cent or one dollar coins be offered?
If I ask this question, it is because nothing in this bill indicates at what price those dollar coins will be sold.
For instance, clause 9 of the bill reads:
"396". Every one who, with intent to defraud, knowingly utters
(a)	a coin that is not current, or
(b)	a piece of metal or mixed metals that resembles in size, figure or colour a current coin for which it is uttered,
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
Therefore, the only thing this bill contains is a warning against substitutes.
At the present time, in Viet Nam, Canadian soldiers can exchange the American dollar for 70 units of that country's currency on the regular market, and it may go up to 130 and even 140 units.
As for the mtehods used in the Polish Socialist Republic, in the daytime tourists may obtain at the banks or at foreign exchange offices 25 zlotys for one United States dollar, but after 9 p.m., through private dealers, tourists may get as much as 90 zlotys for one United States dollar.
This is known the world over as the black market. This is a criminal offence under the law; anyone found guilty is liable to 2 years in jail.
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins
The situation here is rather strange, as last summer some had the nerve to offer one dollar silver coins, minted to commemorate our centennial, at $3 each. Many people in my area, students, teachers, three credit union managers, two managers of bank branches, in short people from all classes of society had asked me to get them a few of these silver dollars. I went to the mint, here in Ottawa. I was told I was two days late. So I went to the bank, and they told me that the very small quantity they had received was long since gone. But they were able to refer me to two Ottawa dealers who nonetheless had silver dollars to sell and still do.
Even today these Ottawa dealers, and other American dealers as well, are still offering us silver dollars at unheard of prices. I know that it is too late to remedy the situation, but I would like the minister to take this opportunity to tell us how many fifty cent and one dollar coins were minted to commemorate centennial year.
In addition, for the good of the people, I would like the minister to tell us also how the distribution of those coins was made and by what organizations. How many coins are held by the public and how many are still unsold in stores? I would also like the minister to tell us if that business should really be made legal in our country? In addition, I would like to know how many middlemen took part in that little scheme which finally pushed the price of a centennial dollar up to $3, as I said a while ago? I would like to know what the minister thinks about that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in discussing Bill S-23, as a Social Crediter I think all members of my party and fellow Social Crediters will welcome the announcement regarding the coining of money of less intrinsic value using a metal that is equally durable, if not more so, but worth considerably less on the market for its own sake than silver. We welcome this step because obviously the only quality that money should have is durability, and the only real use to which it should be put is in the exchange of goods. If we find it being purchased for its own sake or being saved and kept as a hedge against inflation, then there is something wrong with the state of the economy and with our regard for and attitude toward money itself.
I have to disagree with the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) because after the
February 8, 1988
6506	COMMONS
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins experience of our centennial year I think it would be wise if the government never again got into the business of producing memorial coins and simply refused to make them for numismatic or any other purposes. I say this because it has already been pointed out to the house by various members that there has been a vast disappearance of thousands, if not millions, of coins that were purportedly designed to come into the hands of the Canadian public as souvenirs or mementoes of centennial year but ended up making an extremely handsome profit for some individuals and dealers, people who remain unidentified but who certainly were not the mass of the Canadian people.
I received early last year, as I am sure most hon. members did, requests from individuals who wanted to know where centennial silver dollars could be obtained. On making inquiries I was told that the coins could be obtained at the chartered banks and all people had to do was make application for them. I was told that, admittedly, the number would be limited for each individual but they could probably obtain at least two apiece if they made application for the coins. Certainly very few of these coins ever got to western Canada through the chartered banks. When people inquired over and over again they found they were absolutely unobtainable. Yet we saw them blossoming out in blocks of plastic in various shops dealing with this type of souvenir, so they were obtainable by certain people.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
One of the Ottawa newspapers pointed out a few months ago that anyone who had enough foresight to obtain a sack of one thousand 50-cent pieces back in the spring could have made a profit of around $5,000 on them by now. Again I do not know how one went about obtaining them. I do not think it was our duty as members of parliament to try to go through the labyrinth to obtain a thousand or so of these coins to carry back to our constituencies and distribute them there, but unless we did I can think of no other way by which they could have been put into the hands of individuals who wanted to collect them.
The items which were quoted from coin magazines yesterday indicating the availability of these coins outside the country are, a sad and sorry commentary on the government entering into the coin business. It is a strange thing that when, for example, certain individuals wish to collect service medals the

government refuses to part with them even when they have surplus stocks, and have not even considered registering bona fide collectors of such items. Yet we know that the government has been in the business of minting centennial dollars for souvenir purposes, which had the effect of making some individuals much more wealthy than they should be.
The situation is much more critical with regard to the coining of the gold dollar-and the regulations in the act cover this-because in view of the great urgency in the minds of the public to reduce the use of gold in modern currency, this is the last thing that any civilized, modern, developed government should be doing with currency. There is heavy pressure on the monetary authorities of the world to permit an increase in the price of gold, to double or treble its value. Canada has joined its friend and ally, the United States, in opposition to that move because the effect on world trade would be disastrous and would give aid and comfort to certain countries which have endeavoured to frustrate the development of the free western world.
The country which would gain the most from an increase in the price of gold would probably be the Soviet union. Such a move would also be a tremendous boost to France which in the past few years has done all it could to turn its United States dollars into gold rather than to hold its reserves in that currency. So we have opposed the move to increase the price of gold but at the same time the government, in our centennial year was engaged in the minting of a $20 gold coin along with other coins amounting to $1.91 which were put into a set and sold for double the value the $20 gold coin gave to the set. While opposing an increase in the price of gold on the one hand we have tacitly suggested that the price of gold should be far higher than it really is on the other. It has been a confusing effort at a time when, through the International Monetary Fund, spokesmen have told us that they have endeavoured to eliminate the use of gold in the monetary system.
This policy was supposed to be ratified by member countries of the International Monetary Fund over the next two years, and it will be the job of their parliaments to endeavour to convince their people and the people of the world that there is no relation between the value of gold and the worth of money. It will be much harder to put that idea across so long as the Canadian government continues to
CMr. Johnston.]

point out that the value of gold is far above $35 an ounce when it is being used for coinage.
I should like to mention one other point. In the minister's statement yesterday reference was made to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the acquisition or purchase of securities of that organization by the Minister of Finance for the Canadian government at a good rate of interest. If the rate of interest is good, then the interest which the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development is charging throughout the world is probably far too high.
We know that some countries which have borrowed from organizations such as the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development have reached the point where they have had to continue borrowing in order to meet the interest charges on the loans they already have, and that no reconstruction and development can take place because these countries have all they can do to keep their heads above water as they pay the interest charges to the organization. Here again the developed nations should change their approach toward the supplying of credit to and the financing of undeveloped nations because so far all their efforts through such organizations as the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development have succeeded only in widening the gap at an accelerating rate between the rich and the poor nations. Although we may congratulate ourselves on the fact that the purchase of these securities is providing a good rate of interest to this country, we should at the same time question very seriously the whole approach because it can only exacerbate an already extremely difficult situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to discover that the program to support the U.S. dollar on which the minister has embarked also meets the Social Credit philosophy and that the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston) believes that this program has encroached into the numismatic field. Frankly, I thought it was a rather strange type of operation that Canada, which has a large quantity of gold and silver for sale, should tie itself to United States financial policies. Yet this has been done and will probably be extended.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Although I do not see anything wrong in doing so, it is probably true that coinage should never be minted to be melted for
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins industrial use. The production of coins has some value. For that reason it would be foolish for the mint to be minting coins while industrial users were melting them down for industrial purposes. However, this has been done in the United States. It was done not because of the value of the coinage but because the United States government pegged the price of silver at a level at which the industrial community could not advantageously buy it from industrial sources so they purchased it from the treasury. The United States government has pegged silver at $1.29. Silver purchased on the London market by industrial users in my area is running as high as $2.04. For this reason, I believe the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke is probably right. I believe this only points up the fact that the price at which the United States government has been forced to peg the silver dollar is an artificial one with which they cannot hope to live but which we probably have to take into consideration.
We can do one of two things with our silver coins. We can either decrease the silver content or increase the size of the coin. The minister is suggesting in this bill that we do both. There are many people in the world today who will buy any kind of junk and call it antiques. They pay a high price for these antiques. Peculiar things happen even in the normal course of business. My brother has a tractor which he has had for a great number of years but on a number of occasions he has been offered more for this Farmall-H than he paid for it, not as an antique but as a trade-in. This seems to me a rather odd situation, particularly when that Farmall-H still does the job it was intended to do and yet commands a higher price in the market today than he paid for it. The same situation applies to used furniture.
I could refer to another field of government endeavour, the production of stamps. We find certain countries in the world that can exist on the revenue from manufacturing stamps. They do not have to go into any other field of endeavour. These countries turn out nice looking stamps which collectors pick up, thus providing sufficient revenue for some of these small countries to take care of their needs without taxation. We in Canada are issuing many new stamps and are finding this a lucrative field. Even in the currency field the minister is now proposing that we set up a factory-type operation and that we mint coinage for other countries. I presume we will
6508	COMMONS
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins also manufacture bank notes on a custom basis.
Since I do not believe in Social Credit philosophy I do not see anything wrong with the minting of gold coins if we are going to get in return twice the amount of money we paid for the gold that is in the coin. This does not seem to me to be a foolish operation. If the government would get out of some other operations and go into the manufacture of gold coins, possibly they could reduce the deficit twice as fast. If we can get $2 for each silver dollar, this would seem to me to be a good arrangement.
I am well aware of what happened in connection with United States currency. We talk about supporting the International Monetary Fund, and probably there is a necessity for that because we live in a community of nations. The United States has been turning out scrip in various countries which they never intend to redeem. Much of the currency the United States has put into Viet Nam they never expect to see again, and for that reason this money is really scrip such as armies operated on during the last war. This money is of value only for trade and the United States hopes that operation will be a one-way street.
Canada is being asked to back the United States government. The International Monetary Fund is now being asked to substitute for gold silver certificates and other forms of hard currency, a unit that will probably not be based on the United States dollar. Most countries of the world have lost faith in the United States dollar. There will be a new unit which the government of Canada and the 63 other nations involved in this operation will develop. I represent a gold mining community which has existed for many years on gold selling at $35 per ounce when everyone knows that the price of gold in the free market is much higher. The United States government set the price of gold at $35 and, incidentally, limited the right of United States citizens to hold gold. Many of these people are buying gold and holding it in Swiss banks as a hedge against the devaluation of their own United States dollar. Whenever there is a run on the United States dollar these people are probably undermining their own currency to a great extent.
Personally, I cannot see anything wrong with what the Canadian government decided to do in coining centennial presentation sets. I congratulate the government upon taking this step. Now that they have taken this step and realize the advantages of the operation, I

DEBATES	February 8, 1968
strongly urge the government to extend it. I am glad the government has adopted what might be called a socialistic way of thinking by deciding they are not going to allow other people to decide what is good for them. I think it is true that most Canadians who wanted to buy a silver dollar had no intention of carrying that silver dollar around in their pockets. In my opinion, Canadians who bought silver dollars did so with the idea of presenting them to children as souvenirs. I suppose they hoped that if the child kept the silver dollar long enough it would be worth $8 or $10 by the time the child wanted to spend it. I am of the opinion the Canadian government should consider the segment of the population that wants to save money by stuffing it under the mattress, so to speak. This $2.5 million worth of coins does not seem to me to be too large a number of silver dollars. I do not know where they will end up, perhaps in the Bank of Canada, but I doubt it. I do not believe they would ever get back to the tellers in local banks.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I doubt that these silver dollars find their way back to the bank in the same way that old bills do. Many of us who get these 50-cent pieces in change drop them in a dresser drawer and save them. If you take them to the bank you find that the teller has a list of people who want to get 50-cent pieces. Since I have been interested in collecting coins I have noticed that you seldom find a worn silver dollar or a worn 50-cent piece. This indicates to me they are not used in normal trading. I feel the government should be fair to the public and indicate why they are restricting the use of these coins and why they are so opposed to the collection of coins. Perhaps one answer lies midway between two very good reasons, reasons which might be underlined by outlining certain steps the government has power to take. Probably one of the reasons is that coin collectors in Canada have an edge on buying methods and have been able to affect large transactions in silver for coinage purposes in the United States. There was an example in a newspaper of a three-ton truck load of silver that was transported to the United States to meet a shortage of coins for vending machines.
The second reason is probably the market that has developed for coinage received from the mint distributed in bags of silver in mintlike condition. The bags were distributed not to the general public but to vending machine operators and for numismatic purposes. These
February 8, 1968
COMMONS DEBATES	6509
coins then find their way into various outlets that sell them back to Canadians at a high profit.
I do not think that the government should become involved in this type of trafficking. On the other hand, I think the minister must explain why he has discontinued the sale of $1.90 worth of coins, not $1.90 worth of silver but face value, in cellophane bags priced at $4. I realize there have been some abuses of these sales, but surely these can be overcome and this type of transaction continued.
I should also like to say that I am of the opinion that the public should be told once and for all that the Canadian government really has no coinage policy in any way, shape or form. In fact the government is following the United States system and is anxious not to do anything that would rock the U.S. dollar. If this is true then perhaps we should link our currency with United States currency.
Some people have suggested that the currency of the International Monetary Fund should be based on the U.S. dollar. Representatives of the Canadian government who attended the recent meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Rio were surprised to find that many countries did not support that suggestion. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if the Canadian government is prepared to support such a proposition it should give leadership in developing a new International Monetary Fund unit that is more compatible with the wishes of its members.
I still feel that there is a place for silver coinage. There is a role for industrial silver in the production of coinage and this role should be perpetuated. We do not want to be put in the position where every industrialist in Canada has to go through a sort of reverse operation, with the mint melting down his coinage and turning it into silver and then melting down the silver and turning it back into coinage. Also, collectors of coinage should still have access to the coin market so they can buy silver dollars or 50-cent pieces, and that access should be guaranteed. The cut-off date should be in September instead of without warning early in the year.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the part of the bill that provides for the transfer of the mint or part of its operations from the city of Ottawa. I think the minister will agree there is an historical connection between the capital of the nation and the minting of money. The capital is the place where the mint should be situated, although I realize
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins that in the United States there is a mint at Pittsburgh and also at Denver. However, there is some historical background to that situation.
I think the argument about relocating the mint has been carried to the extreme during the last few months, so much so that we could find ourselves locating the mint in an area over which Canada had no control. This could mean that instead of minting our own money we would have to get somebody else to do it. This would be a ridiculous situation. I suggest that historically the mint should be in the national capital, and that historical right should be protected.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPOSITION OF COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the introduction of this bill by the
6510	COMMONS
Amendments Respecting Composition of Coins minister. Its main feature is the change in the type of metal used to strike coins for the government of Canada. I think no metal is more representative of Canada than nickel. As you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, Canada supplies the world with better than 65 per cent of its demand for nickel. Over 50 per cent of that production originates in the riding I represent, the city of Sudbury. The whole economy of the city is based on the mining and refining of this metal and for these reasons I am pleased to see the minister introduce into the coinage of our country a metal more in keeping with the job coinage has to do. In many of its qualities nickel is superior to silver or gold. It can stand a great deal of wear, unlike more precious metals which are subject to loss of weight and disfigurement when used in coinage. Nickel is not only valuable but tough and difficult to work. I am sure the coins produced from it will stay in circulation much longer than the conventional coinage of the past.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
There is, of course, a certain magnetism in the precious metals which tempts people to withdraw them from circulation and hoard them. This is a romantic inclination felt by many people. If we turn to a more ordinary metal such as nickel the tendency to hoard might be reduced with beneficial effect on the amount of coinage in circulation. I recall that not too long ago there was a severe shortage of metal coins and the mint was unable to turn new ones out in the quantities required.
I am not against the purchasing of these coins for commemorative purposes. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has pointed out that a one dollar coin made 50 per cent of silver would have a silver content worth 88 cents. I see no reason for not making those dollar coins out of nickel. They would probably have a real value of 15 or 20 cents, but dealers could still sell them for the figure my hon. friend mentioned and the profit to the treasury would be even greater.
We must remember, too, that these coins have to be carried around in our pockets. From time immemorial man has tried to simplify the business of carrying money around. At one time coins consisted of large stones with holes in them and it took an ox-cart to move them from one place to another. Today, in Canada, we have reached a point at which relatively large sums can be carried around as coinage without too much inconvenience.

DEBATES	February 8, 1968
The new coins envisaged by the minister will be 13 per cent lighter than the present coins and easier to carry to this extent. The substitution of nickel in the one dollar coin will lead to a 30 per cent reduction in weight. This will in turn lead to other economies. The minister has estimated that to express these coins across Canada costs $285,000. Thus, if we bring about a reduction in weight amounting to 13 to 30 per cent there is bound to be a considerable saving in shipping costs right off the top.
Many people collect coins which have been disfigured in the course of the original stamping. They will pay thousands of dollars for a 50-cent coin which has a dot in a certain spot. Not unnaturally, there are some individuals who disfigure coins in an attempt to make an ordinary 50-cent piece into a rare one. Unlike nickel, silver is an easy metal to work. Its melting point is around 1,200 degrees. The melting point of nickel is between 2,600 and 2,800 degrees. Thus, anyone who wishes to disfigure a coin made of pure nickel has an extremely hard job on his hands.
I should like to comment on one further proposal in the legislation before us. In referring to the proposed location of the mint the bill says it must remain in the national capital region. I consider that the striking of coins is a manufacturing process. I see no relation between the location of the mint and the location of the parliament of Canada. speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Trudeau for the second reading of Bill No. S-18, to amend the Publication of Statutes Act.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION TO PRESCRIBE FORM AND MANNER OF PRINTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was some debate on this bill last November. I have noted the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) at that time and I also took the trouble to read his testimony before the Senate committee which considered this bill. While I do not want to take up too much time of the house, I believe, considering the expressed purpose of the minister in bringing forward this bill, that he is doing more harm to his cause than good.
The simple situation will be that if this intent is carried into effect every lawyer in Canada will be faced with a doubling of the size of the books with which he is dealing, a doubling of the size of the statutes and the field through which he must search in any book to which he refers. I want to make it plain that I have no particular objection to attempting to further the use of the French language in parts of Canada or the use of the English language in parts of Quebec. However, I do not think it can be argued that the method now suggested by the minister is the only way to do it.
I do not think there is any validity in the argument that the minister seems to suggest, namely, that by doing it in this manner there will be more justice for French speaking Canadians because copies of the statutes will be available in the French language. There is absolutely nothing wrong with statutes being printed in English, and in French, with both volumes being available so that one or the other may be used. I cannot imagine a case coming before any court in the land where the trial will not be held in one language or the other.
As a matter of fact, I am sure that in the courts in most parts of this country you will find that English is used almost exclusively, and in some other courts French is used almost exclusively. For the odd, exceptional case the statutes will be available in the other language. Therefore the necessity of having the other language in the road at all times is going to be irksome. Instead of making our second language a cultural heritage which we
February 8, 1968

will like, treasure and enjoy, it will become an irksome nuisance to those trying to follow their professions in the best way they can. Certainly it would not promote either unity in the country or the further spread of bilingualism if one language were to become irksome and a nuisance in any part of the country.

I think it is perfectly proper to point out that it will be more expensive to print bilingual statutes, not just for the government but for everyone across Canada who refers to them, because if the statutes are printed in the manner suggested by the minister we will have to pay the cost of both sets. The government will have to pay the cost of printing both sets, and each individual in Canada will have to assume the cost of both whether or not he uses them. The idea of finer print bothers me. Certainly legal work is hard on the eyes because it requires constant reading and reference to statutes and case books.
I am amazed that the Minister of Justice is setting out to reduce the size of print in order that both languages may be contained in the same book because in this way he may create difficulties for lawyers across Canada. I believe that many lawyers, especially those getting on in years and having trouble with their eyes, might take this as a personal affront. I do not want to sound as if I were getting too close to that age but as I wear glasses I think I can speak with some authority on this subject. To that I say that it seems to me that ten times more often the French version would be used in order to confuse the issue if a lawyer felt he was losing his argument. I do not think much would be gained by it.
While in the city of Edmonton there are not many bilingual lawyers, I have often appeared before a bilingual judge and have been opposed by a bilingual counsel. Yet I have never heard them refer to a French version for assistance. In fact, I suggest that in many cases the judge would be displeased with what I consider would be an additional complication, particularly in view of the fact that there can be no literal translation of either language. Therefore resorting to another language would in most cases be an added complication rather than assisting in understanding the legislation.
I think the strongest argument used by the minister in favour of this measure is based on his feeling that it would assist in the spread of bilingualism in Canada and that it would give the French speaking people in western areas, for example, a greater feeling of security in the knowledge that the statutes are available in their own language. It has been my feeling for some time, which has been confirmed by some friends of mine who are concerned about the lack of understanding in western Canada of the views of French Canadians on the subject of bilingualism, that this subject has not been taken seriously enough here in Ottawa. Therefore, a vast majority of lawyers in Canada deal in one language most of the time, and whether or not a lawyer is fluently bilingual he knows before going to the court in what language a case will be conducted. In such cases the second language is really redundant. Yet on every occasion when a lawyer goes to court he will have to carry with him statutes in both languages, which may perhaps be a nuisance and irksome to him. He would have the constant reminder that his books were costing him more, that they were taking up more room on his shelves and that the paper was thinner. He would have the constant reminder that he must try to read finer print. All of these constant and irksome reminders would serve to recall to the people of this country that we are a bilingual nation. I feel that he expressed, during this conference, a philosophy we can trace back to the testimony he gave before the Senate committee on banking and commerce. We really find in it the essential basis on which will inevitably rest the Canadian unity that we are on the point of achieving. If it does not yet exist to the extent that the existence of a Canadian ideal could be generally recognized, it is precisely because the French fact has never been accepted, in some parts of the country, as a typically Canadian asset.
When listening to the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) we know that he no doubt speaks with deep conviction and sincerity, but he represents that very minority group in Canada which has always refused to consider the French fact as one of the

greatest assets which enables the Canadian people to be distinguishable from our neighbours to the south, the Americans. And this is fundamental, if Canadian unity is to be strenghtened for future generations.

There was never any question of forcing a language upon anyone; any attempt to do so would be anti-democratic, and we would then have to condemn such a philosophy, such an attitude.

Thank you. I had the opportunity to speak before several university audiences outside Quebec. There is always a great deal of applause when one says to Canada's younger generation: "The French fact is still the strongest feature that distinguishes you from the Americans". Our young Canadians do not want to become Americans. We have heard Americans visiting Quebec city ask us: "Why don't you join the American flag?"
Why were they asking such a question, Mr. Speaker? Because they could not see any difference between Canada and the United States.
They thought that Canada was a wholly English country, and English the only language in use. But when you say to young English Canadians that the French language and culture are live and active factors in the country, they feel proud. I would like here the hon. member for York-Humber to imitate these feelings of the younger generation and revise the erroneous philosophy to which he holds so obstinately.
Publication of Statutes Act
But why all these words, when we are dealing with a seemingly rather insignificant bill? It is precisely because it has symbolic value. And I am only repeating what the minister said before the Senate committee. There is symbolic value in this. Why print the French text besides the English text?
If you want to consider the political aspect of the question, because the legal interpretation aspect-I will come back to that later- has been strongly pointed out, and besides cannot be ignored under the circumstances, it acquires thereby a symbolic value, for by placing the French version besides the English version there is affirmed to the whole country that we have really bilingual institutions.
In the province of Quebec, there are lawyers practising law in Chicoutimi, Rimouski, Quebec city and distant municipalities where the English language is never used. Yet the statutes of the province of Quebec are printed in both languages. There may be extremists who will question that, but people of good will, serious people willingly accept it. We have the French and English versions side by side in the statutes of the province of Quebec, but we would never think of denouncing that fact as a situation through which we might be unduly coerced. Nobody would think of doing that. The phenomenon is accepted, and we are happy to tell the people of the province of Quebec: "English is a language, and the more familiar you become with the English language and culture, the richer your personality will be".
What we would really like in order that the cultural equality spoken of during the constitutional conference these last few days might become an actual fact, would be for people such as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and the hon. member for York-Humber to say one day: "If we want to enrich the personality of all Canadians, we should all have a better knowledge of the two languages and the two cultures, for that is an important factor in our development and in the enrichment of our personality. There is nothing revolutionary in this theory, Mr. Speaker. That should be accepted.
The legislation before us is intended to allow printing the English text beside the French text. But some members, including the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), argue that it would result in additional expenses. That is obvious, Mr. Speaker.
Simultaneous interpretation in the house is an added expense. Bilingual inscriptions

Publication of Statutes Act and all the translation system cost more money than if we did not need them, as in unilingual countries.
But, as the provincial premiers gathered around the constitutional conference table have proclaimed, what we want to establish is language equality. It is a very symbolic way of acknowledging in practice this principle of cultural and bilingual equality. It is a matter of friendly coexistence between the two great Canadian communities. This is the only way, Mr. Speaker, to make Canada a strong and progressive country. In fact, it is the only way to break through the psychological barriers which have been existing for one hundred years, namely that French Canadians do not feel at home when they are outside Quebec.
This is a psychological separatism, a linguistic separatism which inevitably leads to the demand for political separatism. I think that if the hon. members opposite wanted to get inspiration from the spirit which prevailed during the constitutional conference, they would quickly share the spirit which prevails in the bill now under consideration.

That clause 7 of Bill C-104 be amended by inserting in subclause (3) thereof the word "common" between the words "as a" and the word "carrier" In the second line.
February 8, 1968

Subclause (3) would then read:
The company shall, in the exercise of its power under subsection (1), act solely as a common carrier-
We were told at the committee hearing that there is not really any definition of a "common carrier". In the same sense I do not imagine there is a definition of the word "carrier". My purpose in moving the amendment is to make it clear that as far as the words "common carrier" are concerned, they place an obligation on the carrier to make its facilities available to whoever wants to be a customer of that company. I do not know anything about the law in this regard, but I do have the impression that the term "common carrier" is likely to carry the implication that the company is obliged to rent its services, subject to tariffs, regulations and requirements, to any one who legitimately asks for them.
Without the word "common" that implication may not be quite so clear and it is for that reason I move this amendment. I may say I have spoken to the sponsor of the bill in respect of this matter and I understand he has no objection to the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I have no question to raise with regard to the rewording of subclause (4) of the old clause 7, new clause 6, because it really is precisely the same thing passed by the committee. However, there are two important omissions from new subclause (5). I should like to have an explanation from the sponsor. Perhaps he can persuade us that these omissions are not of any consequence.
The original subclause (5) gave a person affected by a decision by the company with regard to a foreign attachment the right to go to the board in an attempt to have that board declare that the foreign attachment is all right because the requirements of the company in a particular case were not reasonable Perhaps I can make that clear.
As I understood the evidence given to the committee it was that any time there is a foreign attachment and the Bell company wants to make sure that the attachment is of such a kind it fits into the circuit, the line or the equipment of the company-

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA

Yes, compatible was the word used. I know nothing about the industry, but it is obvious to anyone that if the attachment is not compatible it might cause trouble to other customers of Bell, or to the equipment Bell has to which the foreign attachment is attached. For that purpose the company was going to have reasonable requirements. We were informed that at the present time the company would make some investigation of the inside and outside of the foreign attachment to make sure it was compatible. According to the wording now in Votes and Proceedings, if I attached something, and I am not likely to, and Bell told me I could not do it, I could go to the Canadian Transport Commission and present my case. If the C.T.C. declared that Bell's requirements were unreasonable, then my attachment would be all right.
The difference in the present wording as I read it, is that there is a sort of general

February 8, 1968
Private Bills
declaration as to whether or not the requirements are reasonable, without the person affected being involved in an appeal to the commission. If I am wrong in that perhaps the sponsor can set me right. It seems to me important that the person affected by the decision of the company should be able to go directly to the commission and have his grievance settled by it, instead of having to read some new requirements which have been promulgated by the commission in lieu of the requirements the company had.
The second change seems to be of perhaps more consequence. The original subclause (5), which is now in Votes and Proceedings, provides for a public hearing in the case of a person affected making an appeal, because the word used was not "may" but "shall". It said that the Canadian Transport Commission shall hold public hearings to determine the effect of the attachment. There is no requirement for any hearing at all as a result of the amendment moved by the sponsor, and there is certainly no requirement for a public hearing.
It seems to me, because this has been done before in other cases, that what this would mean is that Bell would promulgate requirements and send them to the Canadian Transport Commission. The railway committee, or whatever it is called, of that commission would look over the requirements and send Bell a letter saying its requirements were not unreasonable; and that would be that.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Any person who was later affected by a decision of Bell Telephone that a foreign attachment was undesirable would be stuck by a decision of the C.T.C. made in its own executive sessions, or by some officer of the commission on the basis merely of a submission of the regulations of Bell Telephone to the commission.
It may be that I have missed some points, and if so, I would be very glad to be enlightened. But because of these two rather fundamental changes, I personally feel uneasy about the wording of new subclause 5 and I am not ready at the moment to support it unless I am persuaded otherwise.
