Mr. Chairman, this amendment is somewhat complicated and we have just seen it for the first time. It seems to me that it is a new proposition. I for one did not get as excited as some others in the committee about this matter of foreign

attachment generally. I think the hon. member for Waterloo South first proposed this amendment and other members presented their views in brief. The hon. member for Waterloo South felt there should be an appeal for individuals. I pointed out to him the impractical nature of the suggestion, but nevertheless I think the right of appeal should be included in the act.
The amendment says that the Canadian Transport Commission should be involved in this question, whether there is an appeal or not. These are two different propositions. I do not say they are in conflict, but I would not at the moment want to vote for one as against the other. I think the right of appeal that now exists for an individual should be there. I do not think it is practical, I think it will be quite costly, and I doubt whether too many persons will act under this provision. However, I think it is right that it should be there.
The amendment that has been introduced places some onus and responsibility on the Canadian Transport Commission, but we do not know how far they will go in these matters. I suggest that in order to be practical, we retain the old section 5 and make this new provision section 6. Then if there is any conflict in it-and looking at it quickly, I do not think there is-it can be caught in the Senate. The Senate will have noted the debate here tonight.
Then we will have satisfied those on both sides of the question. We will have satisfied those who feel there should be a right of appeal for the individual who believes he is aggrieved. I point out that there is not any third party right per se, anyway, in these foreign attachments. But if an individual feels he has a case, he should have a right of appeal.
I believe that now this matter has been raised, even though it is not too practical and will be a costly procedure, it would not hurt to have the Canadian Transport Commission involved in the question. They could look into the matter that has been mentioned by the hon. member for York South-and I recall asking questions about the interpretation of the word "reasonable"-with regard to what are the "reasonable requirements" that may be prescribed by the company.
Therefore in order to avoid an impasse tonight and in an effort to be co-operative, I think it would be possible to leave in the statute the old section 5 and include this amendment as section 6. If there is any conflict, it will be caught in the Senate. Then we will make everybody happy.

Mr. Chairman, I have noted the remarks of the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and I appreciate their concern with respect to the amendment. If I had taken a little more time when dealing with the amendment I would probably have been able to alleviate their concern. However, I think I can do that now.
As I said earlier, there is no change in the substantive provisions as a result of the amendment. The reason is that the right of appeal, the right of third parties, and so on, is provided in the provisions of the Railway Act, and are now the law of the land. These provisions give the Canadian Transport Commission the right to hear appeals. This amendment was made and offered to the committee at the instance of the Department of Transport. I have here a letter from the chief counsel of the department, Mr. Fortier, which I will table if hon. members wish. As I indicated earlier, the amendment was concurred in by the Department of Justice and by Mr. Henry who was a witness before the committee. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I could read Mr. Fortier's letter. It is addressed to the general counsel of Bell Telephone Company and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I enclose herewith as agreed in our telephone discussion of today the draft paragraphs (4) and (5) of clause 7-
That is now clause 6.
-of Bill C-104, as prepared in the Department of Justice.
This matter was raised by the Department of Justice and they felt it would be better legislation and more in conformity with existing legislation if these amendments were made. Mr. Fortier's letter continues:
In connection with the said redraft made by Justice the officers of the said department point out as follows:
"It seems to me-"
I am here quoting what the Department of Justice said.
"-that if subsections (4) and (5) are set out more or less in line with those set out in my redraft, we will have effectively invoked-"
I think this is the important thing.
sections 33 et seq of the Railway Act, including sections 51, 52 and 53. Not only would aggrieved persons be able to complain to the Board and obtain a hearing but so also would the Minister of Transport."
I think this is important, because under the Railway Act the Minister of Transport would

have the right to intervene in this sort of hearing, and he would presumably intervene in the interests of the public, whom he represents as a minister of the crown. That provision was not made in the original amendment of the committee. Perhaps we did not think of it at the time. -in order that paragraphs (4) and (5) of clause 7 meet the legal requirements involved.
I tried to obtain a copy of the Railway Act just now and I apologize to the committee for not having it here, but I have not been able to obtain a copy yet. Subsection 5 is taken from a provision of the Railway Act applicable to telephone companies in respect of discriminatory tolls and should work for your purposes.

(4)	For the protection ot the subscribers of the company and of the public, any equipment, apparatus, line, circuit or device not provided by the company shall only be attached to, connected or interconnected with, or used in connection with the facilities of the company in conformity with such reasonable requirements as may be prescribed by the company.

speechtext:
This evening, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with several matters relating to the bill. I think we should be very much concerned about the motivation behind this bill. I used to teach school before I entered politics, and during one period in my teaching career I taught French for two and a half months. I taught nothing but French every day for those two and a half months. This fact had nothing to do with my ability to teach French, but it had a great deal to do with the shortage of qualified teachers of French in the province from which I come.

My poor students, I cry when I remember them.

The two and a half months I spent teaching French taught me something about motivation. As is always the experience of anyone who teaches French in British Columbia, I was asked the inevitable question: Why do we have to learn French? Like all teachers, I am sure, of French in that province I gave a variety of reasons to my students: it was a beautiful language; it was useful in promoting national unity; it was a language of great literature; there were millions of people in the world who spoke the language, and so on. I tried to put the best case possible for the task confronting the students.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, I have come to realize that I should have restricted my reasons to only one. I should have answered always in the same way, namely that it promoted national unity-that there was no other reason. I should have reiterated that reason over and over again. Perhaps I should even have had the class learn it in two languages, repeating it after me, chanting it regularly and perhaps singing it. I should have made a slogan out of it. I should then have persuaded all the other teachers of French in the schools in my province to give only that one reason

February 8, 1968

Publication of Statutes Act -that it was something that would increase their patriotism.
If you were to give any other reasons for teaching French in British Columbia you would also have to teach other languages as well. Because there are other languages that are beautiful, that have great literature, that are spoken by millions of people around the world. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the motivation for a bill such as Bill S-18 that has been presented to us must be very precise and equally limited, as in the example I have just given. If we are to deal with this bill and to make any sense of it at all, then it must be in terms of promoting national unity and for no other reason.
This will not be the last bill, Mr. Speaker, of somewhat similar nature to be presented to this house. We know that the minister who deals with corporate affairs, for example, is considering measures which will require all food sold in stores across the country to be labelled in both official languages. If and when the minister introduces a bill to make that the law of the land, he must equally be very careful to state that he is motivated to promote national unity, and for no other reason.
It does not do to say, Mr. Speaker, that the bill before us has anything to do with justice or with seeing that justice is done across the land. If this is the motivation for the bill, then it opens the door to any other language that is spoken by a Canadian. Surely we are not going to suggest for one moment that justice is not done in our courts. If printing the statutes in another language has anything to do with justice, then we would have to print them in a whole variety of languages. I do not think this would be a good idea and I do not think it would lead to national unity, either.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The same applies to the bill having to do with labelling of food products. The Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Turner) has suggested that this be done in two languages for the protection of the public. This contention will not hold water, either, because if the public is to be protected against errors in the purchasing of so basic an item as food, then we should label these products in every language which could possibly be used in this country, since we would wish every citizen to have all the protection we could afford.
Obviously a bill of this kind must be presented on the basis that it contributes to

national unity. If it is presented on this basis it becomes easier for several of us to tell the government and the minister responsible why it will not work and why it will not contribute to that goal.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) has spoken to us as a practising lawyer and indicated the problems which would arise within his profession if the course suggested is followed. He deserves to be listened to by the government and by all hon. members because he is making a valid point. Some of his remarks may apply when, later on, a bill having to do with the labelling of food is presented to us.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) has been praised, and rightly so, for his activities in the last few days during which he has presented his position and the position of the government in connection with constitutional requirements. His presentation has been a gentle one. He moved through most of the conference using what might be described as a velvet glove. Certainly there is no other approach which would lead to national unity and contribute to the acceptance of the two languages throughout Canada. But we must not mistake the velvet glove for the hair shirt, and this is the error with which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona was dealing-the daily irritation which can arise if people are confronted with a second language in a most unlikely and unnecessary place.
If one is to continue to work toward learning a second language the process must ordinarily be a pleasurable one, or at least it must lead to pleasure. The result of printing all the statutes in the same volume in both languages would quickly lead to frustration whether they were printed on the same page or on facing pages, as I understand is intended-this must be the intention because the statutes are already printed in separate volumes in the two languages and are available for use if necessary in our courts.
We in western Canada, and in British Columbia in particular, do not have traditions of hair shirts or self-mortification. If we are to be presented with actions and ideas which contribute to national unity they must be great ideas or pleasant actions, not something which would be a daily irritation. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) suggested to us that this constant reminder would be good for us. This I doubt. I would think the irritation of having to flip through twice the number of pages to find a statute,
February 8, 1968

of being able to read on an open page only-half the amount which would normally be there, would have the result opposite to that intended. Such minor considerations as the quality of the paper, the extra cost might, together with the other inconveniences I have mentioned, lead to a sort of explosion of temper which could become a real factor in the situation in western Canada.
All this is not realized in eastern Canada, either by the press or by the public. The statements of Premier Manning and Premier Bennett represent the thinking of a large proportion of the western population. It might be said that this thinking is not of the quality it should be or that it may be the thinking of people who are not well educated. You can run down the sentiment, but you cannot bring in a bill which would irritate the very people who are probably most receptive to the idea of bilingualism. I cannot think of any group of people I would wish less to irritate in this connection than the lawyers of western Canada, unless it were the school teachers. If in the name of justice, we take this step in connection with the statutes, we could be led to it in a variety of other areas-text books in education dealing with mathematics, for example; food labelling. The possibilities are endless.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
This bill was presented to us a few months ago very late at night in the hope, I think, that at fifteen minutes to ten nobody would realize what it was all about and that it would become law almost by default. However, one or two people did realize some of the dangers inherent in the measure. They protested, and it did not appear on the order paper the following day. I hoped that the initial reaction at that time would have been sufficient to have the bill withdrawn completely. But now it has come back to us, and the timing is unfortunate because it comes at the end of a conference on the constitution and the language problem, a conference hailed in most parts of the country as a great success. At such a time I do not think we need this reminder of how small, how tiny, how irritating a measure can be contemplated in the name of national unity. It is certainly not in the name of justice. Let us not suggest for a moment that that is why it is being presented. If we are going to move toward national unity we will not do so through a host of little irritations, to be repeated over and over again within the next few years. We will have to move on a higher and sounder level than that.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so at some risk of being called a radical, of being called bigoted, but I believe the time has come-and this is a good opportunity on a small, insignificant request made to us by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau)-to take a cold, hard look at Canada and at what Canadianism really means to various Canadians all across Canada.
Speaking about western Canada, Daniel Johnson, as reported in the Gazette of February 6 said he attributed the attitude of the younger provinces, meaning western Canada, to "a lack of Canadianism". Mr. Speaker, on January 23 I was astonished to receive from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) an uncommunicative, curt, abrupt reply to my simple and direct question relating to red circled public servants. My question which appears at page 5841 of Hansard was as to-
-whether the government has under immediate consideration a lump sum payment for those public service employees who are red-circled or other modifications to relieve the hardships of the classification review program?
The reply, couched in haughty and cavalier terms, which have become characteristic of the President of the Treasury Board, was:
Without in any way admitting to the facts contained in the statement that my hon. friend has made I should simply like to answer his question by saying, no.
February 8, 1968

No, no-that is the only answer one gets from the government to any representations on behalf of public servants, present or retired. Unfortunately it is typical of the indifference, the insensibility which the government has displayed toward that unhappy and luckless group of public servants caught in the red-circling program.
That program has caused more resentment, discontent, indeed bitterness and deep-seated anger among a very large number of public servants than any program of which 1 have ever known. The resultant loss of morale will have lasting effects upon the future of the whole public service. Deliver a blow to a public servant's morale, to his pride in his work and service, and the mere removal at a later date of the grievance does not heal the bruise or restore his morale to the status quo ante.
My question was prompted by the knowledge that early in January, 1968, the Public Service Alliance of Canada had made vigorous representations to the Treasury Board that a lump sum payment of 4 per cent be granted to every employee in the administrative and administrative support categories who, on October 1, 1967, were still red-circled. The curt and blunt refusal of the President of the Treasury Board illustrates with what disdain and superciliousness he has treated serious representations by the largest public service organization, how impervious he is to sensible and logical arguments, how unconcerned, unfeeling and callous is the government to the plight of the red-circled employees.
The recent across-the-board increase is no answer to this problem. Indeed it is the strongest argument in favour of the action sought by the Public Service Alliance. When he replies, I should like the parliamentary secretary to be most explicit in making clear that the recent general increase is no solution or assistance for the red-circled employee.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that action taken by the government in November, 1966 is an exact precedent for the proposal I now make. Then a pay supplement for red-circled employees was authorized, such supplement amounting to a 4 per cent lump sum payment of the salary rate as of September 30, 1965. This was intended to provide financial relief to offset the increases in the cost of living for the period October 1, 1965 to October 1, 1966. Since October 1, 1966 the increase in the cost of living has been about six points. Consequently, if the government was right in providing a 4 per cent lump sum payment in
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion 1966, the case is now irresistible and unanswerable for a new lump sum payment designed at least to maintain the real salaries of red-circled employees.
It is no answer to say that the number of red-circled employees has been reduced to about one half the number that existed in November, 1966. If the Treasury Board had done its job, there would be none by this time. This festering sore in our public service would have been totally eliminated.
Some departments are much worse than others. I consider, for example, the discrimination against employees in the checking and refunds branch of the Department of National Revenue, or among the classification of buyers to the Department of Defence Production, constitutes a reproach, a burning shame to the public service. I could mention other branches; branches in national defence, the post office and many other departments where large numbers have been and are still prejudiced.
I point out, as I have done on many occasions in the past, that the fault is not that of the red-circled employee. The classification of his position was established, not by himself but by the old civil service commission. How it can be alleged that the old commission was so dead wrong in so many thousands of cases in past years, but the enlightened gentry of the Treasury Board are infallible today, passes my understanding.
It is the individual public servant who must pay the penalty for the mistakes of others, with resultant breakdown of morale, grave loss to the public at large and deplorable impairment of the public interest. The real answer is to divorce the red circle from the present incumbent; to allow the present incumbent to enjoy all the normal increases and other benefits but to reduce the status and classification of the position effective only when it is next filled. I recognize that a lump sum payment would be only a palliative, but at least it is a measure of justice for the red-circled. On that basis I urge it upon the government.

EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN TEACHING IMMIGRANT CHILDREN

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN TEACHING IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) urging the government to be of some assistance in providing education for the children of immigrants is obviously a good one. What strikes me, personally, about the matter is the fact that in the few years I have been around parliament, representing a riding as I do which is one of the more cosmopolitan ridings in Canada, and having a good deal of exposure to the aspirations and requests of those newly arrived in Canada, I must say this question has never really arisen. I am not aware of its having been raised by anybody in our immigration committees, when we were discussing immigration problems. Perhaps' this is because the people who arrive in this country with young families have never really made the education of their children an issue. I do not believe many
representations have been made in the constituencies, or surely one member would have raised this point before. Perhaps these newly arrived people feel that their children are young enough to be integrated into the school system and, by working harder than native born children, can soon catch up. This problem has never been in the forefront before.

maintopic: EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN TEACHING IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext: It is now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN TEACHING IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext:
Yes, it is now. This does not necessarily mean it is not a problem to which we should give attention and to which we should give assistance. I think it is worthy of consideration. I know the minister's attitude is to get the proper facts and figures in relation to the number of children, teachers and facilities available in order to determine what our program should be in this particular area. This will take some time. I believe the minister has had talks with Mr. Davis, the minister of education for the province of Ontario, in connection with assistance for this type of thing. I feel that the province is involved to a degree in this whole venture. Certainly the research facilities they have, in terms of educational facilities and so on, would be required, so I think the whole area requires co-operation with the provinces. To my knowledge, there has been at least one meeting between Mr. Davis and the minister concerning this problem. They are working on it now to see whether or not something can be done.
As to numbers, and how misleading they can be, my attention is called to a headline in the Toronto Telegram for February 8, 1968 which reads, "18,000 Immigrant Children just a Guess." Apparently the school board started to look into this figure and became rather incensed at the looseness with which figures had been quoted. I should like to quote a couple of paragraphs from this article:
Toronto school trustees are looking for 18,000 new Canadian children who were suddenly at a committee meeting yesterday.
The children, according to statements made last week by board of education chairman Ying Hope, need special English classes but aren't getting them because Toronto can't afford it.
The poor English is not mine in this case, it is the Toronto Telegram's.
Yesterday's new Canadian committee meeting learned, however, that the figure was a guess and that school officials don't really know the annual cost of special English classes.

INDIAN AFFAIRS-CANCELLATION OF SCHOOL PROJECT, CAPE CROKER RESERVE Mr. John Loney (Bruce): Mr. Speaker, on February 7, as reported at page 6465 of Hansard, I submitted to Your Honour that the question I had put to the minister of Indian affairs was indeed urgent. It is now my intention to substantiate my contention that immediate action must be taken to reverse the decision of the department of Indian affairs to cancel the construction of the proposed separate school at the Cape Croker Indian reserve.
The situation that the Indian people are protesting, Mr. Speaker, is best described in this article that appeared in the Montreal Gazette for February 6. It was published on that date under the heading "Indian parents protest school" and reads as follows:
Parents of 90 Roman Catholic children at the Indian reserve here, 40 miles north of Owen Sound, are threatening to take their children out of three buildings which have been used as a school for the last 10 years although they have no water or toilets.
May I correct one point here, Mr. Speaker. There are water and toilets, but there is an inadequate water supply.
The parents plan a protest meeting February 12. They claim federal funds slated for construction of a new school this year have been withdrawn.
Fred Purser, Bruce county Indian agent, said government funds have been cut back despite definite "promises" to build the school this year. 

Joseph Akiwenzie, chief of the Cape Croker band, said the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is "beating around the bush" and "has been promising the school for 10 years."
Rev. O. H. LaBelle, parish priest of the reserve, said records kept by a teacher at the parish hall three years ago showed that the oil heater in one building rarely provided a temperature as high as 60 degrees.
"Most of the time the temperature was 50 degrees and small children were forced to draw their feet up on the seats to keep warm," he said.
"They also had to go outside in the cold to unheated toilets."
This house will agree, Mr. Speaker, that this is indeed a deplorable and unnecessary situation. I must say, with respect, that the departmental officials are aware of the existing accommodation and of the need to provide proper and comfortable facilities conducive to an atmosphere of learning. Until the last few weeks the parents of the children concerned were willing to accept temporary accommodation. Weather conditions, coupled with a deterioration of the three buildings now proven to be inadequate, has moved the parents to protest the circumstances.
My contention that there must be immediate action is supported by a statement of the director of education for the Indian affairs branch. The statement was printed in the Telegram for February 7, appeared under the heading "Ottawa to insulate school", and says:
The federal government has ordered an emergency supply of insulation to keep children from shivering in 50-degree temperatures at the Roman Catholic school on the Cape Croker Indian reserve near Owen Sound.
According to Hansard for February 7 I have already stated that the matter is indeed urgent. This article supports that claim in its reference to the fact that the federal government has ordered an emergency supply of insulation. The article continues:
Students have been wearing snow boots and leggings in the school, a converted church hall, to keep warm.
The building's only source of heat is a single oil stove.
Robert C. Davey, director of education, Indian affairs branch of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, said yesterday the insulation should reach the school "within the next two or three days."
"We've bypassed the procedure of calling for tenders because of the need for immediate action"-
I reiterate, Mr. Speaker-the need for immediate action.
At the outset of my remarks I stated it was my intention to substantiate the need for
February 8, 1968
immediate action. Mr. Davey said he learned of the problem at the school when he received a letter last week from a parent at the reserve. He is reported to have said: "Last fall, when the hall was converted into a classroom we added insulation, a heating unit and storm windows. We did not know these changes were insufficient."
In making representation on behalf of those concerned at Cape Croker, my argument is that these stop-gap measures can no longer be continued. This case goes back to 1958 when a decision was made to construct a new school for both Protestant and Roman Catholic children. Later the plans were altered and a smaller school for Protestant children was completed in 1964, the understanding at that time being that when a building site had been chosen a separate school would be built. In November of last year, according to the information provided me, departmental officials consulted the sisters who staff the schools and put forward plans for the proposed new school upon the understanding that construction would soon commence.
Now the department has reconsidered its intention, claiming that other projects take precedence. I ask the minister to explain to the parents concerned and to the people of Cape Croker what priorities take precedence over the proven need for adequate educational facilities and accommodation by the children of this Indian reserve.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN TEACHING IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext:
It has not
been my privilege to visit Cape Croker but this is probably understandable because I believe we have 2,200 Indian reserves in Canada. I have been on a number of them.
This arises from resentment on the part of the people on that reserve because other areas are being given priority over them when it comes to improving the capital plant needed for education, housing and so on. I believe every member of this house is aware that at the present time we are by comparison spending a fantastic amount of money on Indian affairs. The budget given me in the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion current year for Indian affairs was $122 million. In 1945 it was $5 million. This year we are spending $58 million on education alone. I would defend this because I think it is the first place to spend money in Indian affairs. We have in the current year expended $9,600,000 on the improvement of buildings and in the coming year we intend to build about 84 schoolrooms on the basis of need, taking priority over Cape Croker.
Cape Croker is an area where there are about 80 people presently housed in three buildings. Unfortunately one of the buildings, I am told, is an old church hall the age of which is almost equal to the age of our nation itself. We are doing the best we can to keep it warm during this cold weather and it is our intention in the following fiscal year to build a school there. We have not cancelled anything. We have postponed construction because we are extending our program with respect to Indian affairs. An example is Indian housing, which we have spread, now, over seven years instead of five years, in the amount of $112 million.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I want to assure the hon. member that we are making tremendous improvements on Indian lands and I believe most hon. members are fully aware of this. We have built this year 2,000 houses on Indian reserves. We have put electric light into more than 4,000 Indian houses in the last two years and we have installed sewage and water facilities in some 58 reserves. The difficulty is that when one group of people sees this going on they want to benefit by the same sort of expenditure. I have here, for instance, a wire from the British Columbia region telling me that in other places we are providing Indian houses with gold plated bath tubs. This, of course, is a sort of envy. All I can tell the hon. member is that we are doing the best we can and Cape Croker has a priority, but we have 84 schoolrooms with a higher priority.
